title: Longer decimal is larger
statement: A decimal with more digits after the point is a larger number, because the digits after the point make a bigger whole number.

evidence_patterns.item_shape: compare two decimals where the shorter is larger
evidence_patterns.signature: chooses the decimal with more digits after the point

example.item: Which is larger, 0.5 or 0.25?

title: Adding fractions across numerators and denominators
statement: Fractions are added by adding the numerators together and adding the denominators together, treating the top and bottom numbers as independent whole numbers, the same way fractions are multiplied.

evidence_patterns.item_shape: add two fractions with unlike denominators
evidence_patterns.signature: response numerator = a + c and response denominator = b + d for a/b + c/d, with no attempt at a common denominator
evidence_patterns.notes: Strongest single indicator: the response is smaller than at least one addend, which the learner rarely notices.

evidence_patterns.item_shape: add two fractions with like denominators
evidence_patterns.signature: response numerator = a + c and response denominator = b + b for a/b + c/b; denominators are added even though they match
evidence_patterns.notes: Discriminates from math.frac.add-numerators-keep-denominator, which answers like-denominator items correctly.

discriminators.vs_slip: A slip appears on one item and not on the next of the same shape, and the learner self-corrects when asked to check with a diagram or with 1/2 + 1/2. A holder of this belief applies the rule consistently across unlike- and like-denominator items and defends 1/2 + 1/2 = 2/4 as correct.

vs.math.frac.add-numerators-keep-denominato: Give a like-denominator item. Add-across produces a doubled denominator (1/4 + 2/4 = 3/8); add-numerators-keep-denominator produces the correct 3/4 and only fails on unlike denominators.

title: Bigger denominator means bigger fraction
statement: The fraction with the bigger denominator is the bigger fraction, because the denominator is a bigger number.

evidence_patterns.signature: picks the unit fraction with the larger denominator as larger; on 1/b vs 1/d chooses the one with the larger b

statement: A fraction is simplified by crossing out a digit that appears in both the numerator and the denominator.

title: Comparing fractions by the gap between numerator and denominator
statement: The size of a fraction is decided by how many pieces are missing from the whole; fractions with the same gap between numerator and denominator are equal.

evidence_patterns.item_shape: compare two fractions with the same numerator-denominator gap
evidence_patterns.signature: declares the fractions equal because each is the same number of pieces short of one whole

example.item: Which is larger, 5/6 or 7/8?

evidence_patterns.notes: The gap is an additive comparison; the learner ignores that eighths are smaller than sixths.

evidence_patterns.item_shape: compare two fractions with different gaps where the smaller gap belongs to the smaller fraction
evidence_patterns.signature: picks the fraction with the smaller numerator-denominator gap as larger regardless of denominators

example.item: Which is larger, 2/3 or 7/10?

evidence_patterns.notes: Gaps are 1 and 3; the learner reasons 'two thirds is only one piece away'.

discriminators.vs_slip: Ask the learner to explain. Gap thinkers say 'both are one away from a whole' or 'this one is closer'. A slip comes with no such rule and is not repeated on 3/4 vs 9/10.

vs.math.frac.compare-whole-number-component: On 5/6 vs 7/8 component comparison picks 7/8; gap thinking says equal.
vs.math.frac.bigger-denominator-bigger-frac: On 1/3 vs 1/8 gap thinking compares the size of one piece and often answers correctly; the denominator rule picks 1/8.

title: Comparing fractions by their whole-number parts
statement: To compare two fractions you compare the numerators and the denominators as whole numbers; a fraction with bigger numbers is a bigger fraction.

evidence_patterns.signature: chooses the fraction whose numerator and denominator are both larger

example.item: Which is larger, 4/5 or 5/9?

evidence_patterns.notes: Incongruent item: whole-number ordering and fraction ordering disagree, so the error is diagnostic. Pair with a congruent item (2/7 vs 3/8) which this belief answers correctly; near-perfect congruent accuracy with systematic incongruent errors is the signature.

vs.math.frac.bigger-denominator-bigger-frac: Unit-fraction items isolate the denominator rule. Component comparison also covers non-unit fractions such as 4/5 vs 5/9.
vs.math.frac.compare-by-gap: On 5/6 vs 7/8 gap thinking says they are equal; component comparison picks 7/8.

title: You can only divide a larger number by a smaller one
statement: In a division the bigger number must be divided by the smaller number, so if the divisor is bigger the two numbers should be swapped.

evidence_patterns.item_shape: draw or describe memory after two variables refer to one object
evidence_patterns.signature: draws two separate objects, one inside each variable

example.item:
p = Point(1, 2)
q = p
Draw p and q.
example.expected: Two variables, both pointing to one Point object
example.response: Two boxes, each containing a Point(1, 2)

evidence_patterns.item_shape: predict identity comparison of two variables assigned from one another
evidence_patterns.signature: predicts they are different objects

example.item:
p = Point(1, 2)
q = p
print(p is q)

discriminators.vs_slip: Diagnosed by the drawing or by identity questions; the model is consistent. A slip is a single wrong prediction with a correct drawing.

vs.prog.obj.assignment-copies-object: Assignment-copies is the behavioural prediction; this record is the memory model behind it. Use the drawing task to separate learners who know about references but think assignment copies from those with no reference concept.

conflicts_with.label: An object variable holds a reference; assignment copies the reference

resolved_by.label: An object variable holds a reference; assignment copies the reference

statement: In an expression that mixes strings and numbers with +, the numbers are added together first and the string is attached afterwards.

title: Dividing two integers gives a fraction
statement: Dividing one whole number by another gives the exact mathematical result with a fractional part, whatever the types involved.

evidence_patterns.item_shape: predict the result of integer division in a language that truncates
evidence_patterns.signature: predicts the exact quotient

example.item:
int x = 7 / 2;
System.out.println(x);

evidence_patterns.item_shape: compute an average of integers
evidence_patterns.signature: divides an int sum by an int count and expects a decimal average

example.item:
int total = 7, n = 2;
double avg = total / n;

discriminators.vs_slip: Consistent across items; the learner is surprised by 3 and cannot explain it. A slip is forgetting a cast once while knowing the rule.

conflicts_with.label: Dividing two integers gives an integer result

resolved_by.label: Dividing two integers gives an integer result

title: Assignment states an equation
statement: The equals sign in an assignment states that the two sides are equal, as in algebra, so x = x + 1 is a contradiction and a = b and b = a mean the same thing.

evidence_patterns.item_shape: trace an assignment whose right-hand side uses the variable being assigned
evidence_patterns.signature: declares the statement impossible or leaves the variable unchanged

example.item:
x = 5
x = x + 1
What is x?

evidence_patterns.item_shape: trace an assignment with the variables in the 'wrong' order
evidence_patterns.signature: treats a = b as also setting b from a, or asks which one changes

example.item:
a = 1
b = 2
a = b
What are a and b?
example.response: a is 1, b is 1 (or 'they are now the same variable')

discriminators.vs_slip: Consistent across items; the learner uses the words 'equals' or 'is the same as' and objects to x = x + 1. A slip is a wrong final value with an otherwise correct trace.

vs.prog.var.assignment-links-variables: Linkers accept a = b as directional but expect later changes to b to show up in a; equation believers object at the moment of assignment.
vs.prog.var.assignment-moves-value: Movers empty the source variable; equation believers keep both sides equal.

resolved_by.label: Assignment copies a value into a variable at one moment

title: Assignment links two variables
statement: After a = b the two variables are connected, so whenever b changes later, a changes too.

evidence_patterns.item_shape: trace a change to the source variable after an assignment between primitives
evidence_patterns.signature: reports the destination variable as having the source's new value

title: The computer understands variable names
statement: The name of a variable tells the computer what it is for, so a variable called total will add things up and one called largest will hold the biggest value.

evidence_patterns.item_shape: predict the value of a descriptively named variable that is never updated
evidence_patterns.signature: predicts the value the name suggests rather than the value assigned

example.item:
largest = 0
for n in [4, 9, 2]:
    pass
print(largest)

discriminators.vs_slip: The prediction follows the name on every item, and renaming the variable to x changes the learner's answer. A slip does not depend on the name.

title: Uninitialised variables start at zero
statement: A variable that has been declared but never assigned holds zero, or an empty value, so it can be safely read or added to.

discriminators.vs_slip: A slip is forgetting one initialisation while knowing it is needed. The belief is stated ('it starts at zero') and the learner omits initialisation habitually.

title: A variable remembers every value it has held
statement: A variable stores every value ever assigned to it, so an earlier value can still be read out later.

evidence_patterns.item_shape: trace repeated assignment to one variable and then use it
evidence_patterns.signature: uses an earlier value, or sums the values, instead of the most recent one

example.item:
x = 3
x = 5
print(x)

evidence_patterns.item_shape: accumulate in a loop
evidence_patterns.signature: expects the variable to hold the list of values seen rather than the running total

example.item:
total = 0
for n in [1, 2, 3]:
    total = total + n
print(total)

discriminators.vs_slip: Consistent across items; the learner talks about the variable 'having' several values. A slip is a single wrong trace step.

vs.prog.control.loop-body-variables-reset: Resetters lose values between iterations (total becomes 3); history-keepers retain too many.
